newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain June CPI seen unlikely to spark key rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Spain June CPI seen unlikely to spark key rate cut.

text.p: Spanish June inflation, forecast to be steady or a little higher than May's 1.5 percent rate, is unlikely to prompt the central bank to cut key money rates next week or indeed before the autumn, economists said on Wednesday.

Signals of strong economic growth, particularly on the consumer side, and a seasonal pick-up in inflation over the summer because of the expected tourist boom are firm arguments against a cut, they said.

"Comments from the Bank (of Spain) indicate a much more cautious stance. Growth rates will continue to accelerate to see GDP just over three percent by the end of the year," said Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
"Consumer spending is picking up and there is some evidence indicating prices are drifting up, although pressures are modest."
This should prompt a more cautious stance from the central bank from now on, having cut the key money rate by four percentage points to 5.25 percent in this rates cycle, he said.
One of Spain's wise men, the group of economists who advise the Economy Ministry, said the Bank of Spain was left with very little scope for further reductions in its key money market rate.
"There is now a very little scope to cut interest rate," said Angel Laborda, when asked about monetary policy at a news conference on Wednesday.

The June Consumer Price Index (CPI), due Friday, is expected to be unchanged to slightly higher versus May, for a 1.6 percent year-on-year increase, according to a Reuters average of economists' forecasts.
The core rate, which excludes energy and fresh food, is seen up 0.1 percent on the month for a 1.8 percent year-on-year rise.
This compares with an inflation rate of 1.5 percent on the year in May, sharply down from 3.2 percent in December. The core rate was 1.9 percent in May.
Colin Warren, economist at Tokai Bank in London, saw a small chance for a rate cut at Monday's Bank of Spain repo auction.
"I think they'll hold (money) rates unless the (CPI) number is very good, by that I mean a headline rate of 1.5 percent," he said.
"(But) I think we'll see the effect of falling food prices from last year petering out, so it would be optimistic to see inflation stay the same (this month)," he said.
He agreed that the central bank was concerned about accelerating growth in gross domestic product and its implications for future inflation.

"For the Bank of Spain the dilemma is that the economy is picking up quicker than expected, (and) the deficit has come in better than expected because of GDP growth...(as regards rate cuts) it's a case of what they can get away with," Warren added.

First quarter gross domestic product growth (GDP) was 2.9 percent year-on-year, versus 2.6 percent in the fourth quarter. Private consumption was up 2.8 percent and forecasts are that this trend will be maintained, or even increase.
The central bank might also await a "really strong" indication that Spain will be in at the launch of the single European currency, he added.
Other economists argued that the central bank might focus on aspects such as the budget, which paved the way for a rate cut in the autumn of 1996, as well as European economic convergence factors.

"The only thing that might do it is further interest rate convergence, if investors start to believe even more fervently that EMU is going to go ahead on time," said Gwyn Hacche, economist at HSBC Capital Markets in London.
Not only will the central bank focus on its 1998 two percent inflation target, it also has to bear in mind market confidence, analysts said.

"It's very very difficult if you set a tough target for next year...there's a good backdrop for growth picking up. So the bank has a credibility problem if it continues to cut rates," said Tokai's Warren.
Most analysts see chances of a slight pick-up in inflation during the summer, although they said the CPI was likely to stay under the psychologically important two percent level.

"We think inflation will pick up temporarily in the summer months and afterwards will fall off again. It's possible that it is well below two percent by year-end," said Edita Perieira at Analistas Financieros Internacionales in Madrid. -- Madrid newsroom + 34 1 585 8340
